heading: Rust awaits a real Yon endpoint
summary: A Rust service gets its HTTPClient with `Needs` and awaits it with `.await`. The client trait declares `async fn read(&self) -> BehaviorResult<Greeting>`, and Tachyon writes the method. `GreetingSetup` adds no adapter, so the request goes to the server of the page: the same origin, without cookies. The answer becomes the typed `Greeting` model from `client/models`; an answer of another shape fails with the error code `HTTP_RESPONSE`. A failed request gives the error code of the browser transport, such as `HTTP_STATUS`, and the `?` operator passes it on. `Cached` lets the browser cache answer a read, and after a successful `ClearCache` the next read asks the server again. `OverrideSetup` gives `OverrideClient` its own adapter, and that adapter answers instead of the network. While an `async` method waits, the page reads the fields as they were when the method started, and other calls to the same service wait for it. Removing the component cancels the request. `Retry`, `MaxAtOnce` and `AllOrNothing` belong on a service method; the build refuses them on a client request method. In a native app and in a test unit there is no browser transport: the request fails with `HTTP_MISSING` unless the Setup gives the client an adapter. In a test, a Fake field `std::cell::RefCell<Option<std::sync::Arc<GreetingClient>>>` can supply the client; while it is empty, the service gets a client whose requests the TestSetup adapter answers. The server half of this example is a plain JavaScript controller. A controller in TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Go, Dart, Ruby, Lua or C++ answers in the same way (see Controllers), so this section shows only the browser side in other languages.
